questions.stem: The murder of 14-year-old Emmett Till in Mississippi in August 1955 drew national attention because:
options: it took place during the Montgomery Bus Boycott and was filmed by television crews
his mother held an open-casket funeral and photographs of his body were published
his killers were convicted by a federal court and sentenced to life imprisonment
President Eisenhower sent federal troops to Mississippi to arrest those responsible
questions.explanation: Mamie Till insisted the casket stay open so the world could see what had been done to her son, and Jet magazine published the images. An all-white jury acquitted the two white men accused, who later admitted the killing in a magazine interview.

questions.stem: In 1956, 101 southern members of Congress signed the 'Southern Manifesto'. It:
options: condemned Brown and pledged lawful means to reverse it
called on southern states to comply quickly with school desegregation
proposed a constitutional amendment banning poll taxes in the South
demanded that federal troops be withdrawn from Little Rock, Arkansas
questions.explanation: The manifesto called Brown an abuse of judicial power and encouraged resistance by legal means. It gave political respectability to 'massive resistance' in the South. Little Rock came the following year, in 1957.

questions.stem: The Civil Rights Act of 1957 is significant mainly because it:
options: suspended literacy tests across the South and sent federal registrars into Mississippi
outlawed discrimination in the sale and rental of housing across the whole country
was the first federal civil rights law since Reconstruction, though weak on voting
banned segregation in all public accommodations such as hotels and restaurants in the South
questions.explanation: The 1957 Act created a Civil Rights Division in the Justice Department and a Commission on Civil Rights, but was watered down to pass the Senate. Public accommodations came in 1964, literacy-test suspension in 1965 and fair housing in 1968.

questions.stem: The Albany Movement in Georgia (1961-62) is often judged a setback for King. Which factor best explains its limited success?
options: The police chief avoided open violence and used jails in nearby towns
Local Black residents refused to take part, so King marched almost alone
Federal troops sent by Kennedy broke up the demonstrations within days
The city desegregated at once, leaving the campaign with nothing to protest
questions.explanation: Chief Laurie Pritchett arrested marchers without the brutality that drew national sympathy, and avoided overfilling his jails. King and the SCLC learned from this and chose Birmingham, where confrontation was more likely to expose segregation to the nation.

questions.stem: In his 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (April 1963), Martin Luther King replied to white clergy who called his campaign unwise and untimely. He argued that:
options: Black Americans should separate from white society and build their own institutions
the federal government, not protesters, should decide the pace of desegregation
people have a moral duty to disobey unjust laws, and waiting meant continued injustice
violence was justified in self-defence when the courts refused to protect Black citizens
questions.explanation: King distinguished just from unjust laws and defended nonviolent direct action that openly broke segregation laws and accepted the penalty. He criticised white moderates who preferred order to justice. Separation and armed self-defence were ideas associated with Malcolm X and later Black Power.

questions.stem: Medgar Evers, murdered outside his home in June 1963, was:
options: the NAACP's Mississippi field secretary
a founder of the Black Panther Party
the first Black student at Ole Miss
SNCC's chairman during Freedom Summer
questions.explanation: Evers led NAACP organising and investigations in Mississippi. His killer, a white supremacist, was not convicted until 1994, after two earlier trials ended with hung juries. James Meredith was the first Black student at the University of Mississippi.

questions.stem: The Twenty-fourth Amendment, ratified in 1964:
options: gave the vote to citizens aged 18 or over
outlawed segregated public schools
ended slavery throughout the United States
banned poll taxes in federal elections
questions.explanation: Poll taxes had kept many poor Black and white southerners from voting. The amendment covered federal elections; the Supreme Court extended the ban to state elections in 1966. The voting age was lowered by the Twenty-sixth Amendment in 1971.

questions.stem: In Loving v. Virginia (1967), the Supreme Court:
options: upheld the use of busing to desegregate public schools in the South
ruled that racial quotas in university admissions were unconstitutional
struck down state laws banning interracial marriage
ruled that segregated buses on interstate routes were unconstitutional
questions.explanation: Mildred and Richard Loving had been convicted in Virginia for marrying across the colour line. The unanimous ruling ended such laws in the 16 states that still had them. Busing was upheld in 1971 and quotas struck down in 1978.

questions.stem: The Watts riot in Los Angeles in August 1965 broke out only days after the Voting Rights Act was signed. Historians see its timing as significant because it showed that:
options: southern legal victories did little for poverty and policing in other cities
the Voting Rights Act had been opposed by most African Americans in California
Martin Luther King had moved the SCLC's main campaign to Los Angeles
the federal government had stopped enforcing civil rights laws outside the South
questions.explanation: Watts began after a traffic arrest and reflected anger at unemployment, housing and policing. It pointed to problems of de facto segregation and economic inequality that the laws of 1964 and 1965 did not address.

questions.stem: In 1964 Malcolm X left the Nation of Islam and made the pilgrimage to Mecca. Which change in his ideas followed?
options: He rejected all political action and urged followers to withdraw from public life
He began calling for Black Americans to emigrate to Africa under Nation of Islam rule
He accepted that white people could be allies and worked with civil rights groups more
He gave up Black nationalism and joined King's Southern Christian Leadership Conference
questions.explanation: Seeing Muslims of many races on the Hajj led him to reject the Nation of Islam's teaching that whites were inherently evil. He founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity, still stressing Black pride and self-defence, before he was assassinated in February 1965.

questions.stem: The Kerner Commission, reporting in 1968 on the urban riots of 1967, concluded that:
options: the riots were organised by communist agents and outside agitators from other states
poverty in the cities had largely been solved by Johnson's Great Society programs
the main cause of the riots was the Supreme Court's decision in Brown v. Board
white racism was creating two separate and unequal societies
questions.explanation: Johnson's commission blamed segregation, poverty and white racism and warned the nation was moving towards two societies, one Black and one white. It called for major spending on jobs and housing, which Johnson, focused on Vietnam, largely did not follow.

questions.stem: King's last campaign, the Poor People's Campaign of 1968, shows a shift in his focus towards:
options: ending segregation in the armed forces
economic justice for poor people of all races
voting rights in the rural Deep South
desegregating southern lunch counters and bus depots
questions.explanation: King planned a mass protest in Washington to demand jobs and an end to poverty, joining Black, white, Latino and Native American poor people. He was killed in April 1968 before it began; the protest camp, Resurrection City, achieved little.

questions.stem: In Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education (1971), the Supreme Court:
options: upheld busing students as a way to desegregate schools
struck down busing between cities and their suburbs
banned the use of race in university admissions
ruled that segregated schools were inherently unequal
questions.explanation: Swann allowed federal courts to order busing where schools had been segregated by law. Three years later, Milliken v. Bradley (1974) limited busing across district lines, which protected largely white suburbs from city desegregation plans.

questions.stem: Why did the Supreme Court's decision in Milliken v. Bradley (1974) limit school desegregation in northern cities?
options: It banned all school busing, even within a single district that had segregated by law
It required private schools to admit Black students, causing white families to move
It blocked plans to bus students between largely Black city districts and white suburbs
It overturned Brown v. Board and allowed states to reintroduce legally segregated schools
questions.explanation: The case concerned Detroit, where white families had moved to separate suburban districts. Because suburbs could not be included without proof they had discriminated, city schools stayed largely Black. Brown was not overturned and busing within districts continued.

questions.stem: Violent opposition to court-ordered busing in Boston from 1974 is often used to show that:
options: resistance to desegregation was not only a southern problem
busing had the support of almost all white northern families
the Supreme Court had banned busing in New England states
most Black families in Boston opposed attending integrated schools
questions.explanation: When a federal judge ordered busing to desegregate Boston's schools, buses carrying Black students were stoned and protests continued for years. The crisis exposed de facto segregation and racial tension in the North.

questions.stem: In Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978), the Supreme Court ruled that:
options: private universities were free to exclude applicants on the basis of race
fixed racial quotas were unlawful, but race could be one factor in admissions
all forms of affirmative action in university admissions were unconstitutional
universities must reserve a fixed share of places for minority applicants
questions.explanation: A medical school's set-aside of 16 places for minority students was struck down, but a majority accepted race as one consideration. In 2023, in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, the Court went further and ended race-conscious admissions.

questions.stem: Supporters of affirmative action argued that it was needed to overcome the effects of past discrimination. Opponents most often argued that it:
options: gave white applicants an unfair advantage in jobs and university places
was a policy of the Nation of Islam rather than of the mainstream movement
treated people differently by race, against the colour-blind goal of 1964
had been forced on states by Congress without any decision of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Critics, including some former movement supporters, claimed preferences reversed the principle that race should not count. Supporters replied that equal treatment alone could not undo generations of exclusion. The debate shows how the movement's goals came to be interpreted differently.

questions.stem: In 1972 Shirley Chisholm, the first Black woman elected to Congress, became the first African American to:
options: lead the NAACP as its first national president
seek a major party's nomination for president
serve as a justice of the Supreme Court
be elected governor of a southern state
questions.explanation: Chisholm, elected to the House from New York in 1968, campaigned for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972. Thurgood Marshall had become the first Black Supreme Court justice in 1967.

questions.stem: Which development best shows the growth of Black political power in the decades after the Voting Rights Act?
options: The repeal of the Voting Rights Act by Congress in 1982 as no longer necessary
The election of Black governors in every southern state by the end of the 1970s
The creation of a separate Black political party that won seats in Congress
A large rise in Black elected officials, including big-city mayors
questions.explanation: Black registration in the South rose sharply and thousands of Black officials were elected, including mayors such as Atlanta's Maynard Jackson (1973). Congress renewed and extended the Voting Rights Act in 1970, 1975, 1982 and 2006 rather than repealing it.

questions.stem: Which event of 1983 recognised the movement's place in national memory?
options: The opening of the Lincoln Memorial in honour of the March on Washington
The first election of an African American to the presidency
A law creating a federal holiday in honour of Martin Luther King
The award of the Nobel Peace Prize to Malcolm X after his death
questions.explanation: President Reagan signed the law in 1983 and the holiday was first observed in 1986. King had received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964; Barack Obama was elected president in 2008.

questions.stem: The Los Angeles riots of 1992 followed:
options: a Supreme Court decision to end school busing in California
the arrest of Louis Farrakhan during the Million Man March
the acquittal of police officers filmed beating Rodney King
the assassination of Jesse Jackson during his presidential campaign
questions.explanation: Amateur video of the 1991 beating was widely shown, and the officers' acquittal by a jury in April 1992 set off days of rioting. Like Watts in 1965, it showed anger at police conduct and urban inequality decades after the civil rights laws.

questions.stem: In Shelby County v. Holder (2013), the Supreme Court struck down the formula deciding which areas needed federal approval before changing voting rules. Why do many historians see this as significant?
options: It ruled that the Fifteenth Amendment did not protect African Americans' right to vote
It weakened a key protection of 1965, and some states soon changed voting rules
It restored literacy tests and poll taxes in every state that had used them before 1965
It extended federal preclearance of voting laws to all fifty states for the first time
questions.explanation: Without a coverage formula, preclearance under Section 5 stopped operating. The Court said conditions had changed since 1965; critics argued new restrictions such as strict voter ID laws fell hardest on minority voters. Literacy tests and poll taxes remained illegal.

questions.stem: The Black Lives Matter movement began in 2013 as a social media hashtag after:
options: Barack Obama lost his campaign for re-election to the presidency
the Supreme Court ended affirmative action in university admissions
Congress repealed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 in a narrow vote
George Zimmerman was acquitted of killing the teenager Trayvon Martin
questions.explanation: The phrase was first used by Alicia Garza, with Patrisse Cullors and Opal Tometi. The movement grew after police killings such as Michael Brown in Ferguson in 2014 and George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, when protests spread worldwide, including in Australia.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares Black Lives Matter with the civil rights organisations of the early 1960s?
options: It was more decentralised, organised online rather than by a few leaders
It relied mainly on lawsuits by the NAACP rather than on street protest
It was led by southern Black ministers through a network of churches
It rejected protest and concentrated only on electing candidates to Congress
questions.explanation: Black Lives Matter stressed group-centred, local leadership and spread through networks online, while groups such as the SCLC were closely identified with leaders like King. Its preference for grassroots organising echoes Ella Baker's approach in SNCC.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that the movement achieved more legal and political change than economic change?
options: Segregation and voting barriers ended, but racial gaps in wealth and income remained
Barack Obama was elected president in 2008, and a federal holiday honours Martin Luther King
Congress renewed the Voting Rights Act several times, most recently for 25 years in 2006
The Supreme Court upheld busing in 1971 but limited it across district lines in 1974
questions.explanation: Only the first option sets political and legal gains against continuing economic inequality, which is what the claim compares. The others describe political or legal developments alone, so they cannot show a contrast with economic outcomes.

questions.stem: Historian Jacquelyn Dowd Hall argued for a 'long civil rights movement'. This interpretation challenges the familiar story by:
options: claiming that federal presidents rather than activists drove all major change
treating Black Power as unconnected to the earlier civil rights struggle
extending it back to the 1930s and past 1968, linking it to economic justice
arguing the movement began only with Brown in 1954 and ended with the 1964 Act
questions.explanation: The familiar 'classical' narrative runs from Montgomery to King's death. Hall and others argue this narrows the movement, cutting out earlier labour and left activism and later struggles, and makes it seem finished when many goals were still unmet.

questions.stem: Historians such as Charles Payne, studying Mississippi, emphasise a 'bottom-up' view of the movement. This view stresses:
options: the importance of Cold War foreign policy in ending segregation
the role of northern white liberals in founding the major organisations
the work of local people and community organisers rather than national leaders
the decisions of presidents and the Supreme Court as the main cause of change
questions.explanation: Bottom-up historians argue that sharecroppers, local NAACP members, women and young SNCC workers sustained the movement, while top-down accounts focus on King, presidents and the courts. Most historians now combine the two.

questions.stem: A historian uses a 1965 FBI memo describing Martin Luther King as a threat to national security. The memo is most useful as evidence of:
options: how some federal agencies viewed and sought to undermine it
King's real aims and his private beliefs about communism
how most Americans viewed King at the time of the memo
the success of the Selma campaign in winning voting rights
questions.explanation: Under the COINTELPRO program the FBI surveilled and tried to discredit King and later the Black Panthers. The memo reveals the attitudes and methods of its authors, not King's actual views or wider public opinion.

questions.stem: Which development is the strongest evidence of continuity rather than change in the issues raised by the movement since the 1960s?
options: Protests against police killings in 2014 and 2020 echoed causes of 1960s riots
The election of thousands of Black officials in the South after the Voting Rights Act
The end of legal bans on interracial marriage after Loving v. Virginia in 1967
The creation of a federal holiday honouring Martin Luther King in 1983
questions.explanation: Police conduct sparked unrest in Watts (1965), Detroit (1967), Los Angeles (1992) and again in Ferguson and Minneapolis, showing a long-running grievance. The other options are examples of change.
